newsitem.title: USA: EMU frailty serves up dlr/French play--BoA analyst.
newsitem.headline: EMU frailty serves up dlr/French play--BoA analyst.

text.p: Deepening fissures in Europe's plan to unite under a single currency highlight a very attractive bet on the dollar versus the French franc, according to Bank of America's chief economist in Spain.

Speaking to reporters at a breakfast meeting here, BA's Henrik Lumholdt explained that the dollar would rise against the franc and other European units, but not the mark, should European economic and monetary union (EMU) fail.
"If EMU should blow up, we'll likely have an increase in the mark intra-Europe," said Lumholdt.
"That would eat into dollar/mark, but the franc will still get hurt. So, the optimal strategy is to be long the dollar and short the franc."

While many European nations have made significant progress in paring their federal deficits in an effort to meet the requirements for EMU entry, some have also resorted to budgetary "gimmicks" to improve their official performance, Lumholdt noted.

Should Europe be forced to scrub EMU's proposed January 1999 launch, which Lumholdt considers a 50-percent probability, those gimmicks will be exposed just as the impetus for strict fiscal discipline will disappear.

"The accounting gimmicks will show up and there will probably be pressure in France, Italy and Spain to run expansionary policies, meaning the disinflationary process will no longer be intact," Lumholdt added.

The apparent willingness of the Group of Seven industrial nations to tolerate a slowly rising dollar and the positive carry afforded by higher U.S. interest rates make the dollar a very attractive bet versus the franc, he added.

German popular resistance to a weak common currency supplanting the traditionally firm mark will stop German leaders from striking a deal with their neighbors to overlook budgetary shortcomings and press on with EMU, Lumholdt said.

While many observers consider a delay in EMU equivalent to a death sentence, the would-be EMU partners will have little choice but to delay unless European growth miraculously quickens, Lumholdt said.
"I don't think we've seen enough structural reform in Europe for that kind of growth to happen," he added.
"And while I don't think EMU disappears into nothingness (if delayed), I think the probability of a delay longer than two years is very large," he said.
Hard-line German monetary officials clearly object to Italy's plans to participate in the first round of EMU, Lumholdt noted.
Still reeling from the costly currency unification with East Germany, many western Germans see union with the lira triggering massive transfer payments to Italy, he added.
That effectively torpedoes Spain's efforts to join EMU on the first round, even if the country makes greater progress than Italy toward the entry targets, Lumholdt said.

"Can you allow Spain and not Italy? It's probably not possible. Italy was a founding member of the (European Community) and is a member of the G7. There's a certain amount of prestige involved here," Lumholdt said.
